title: Indian Banks Are Racing to Offer NRIs 5 Per Cent on Dollar Deposits. The RBI Is Picking Up the Tab.
excerpt: The central bank's FCNR window — its biggest since 2013 — could pull $35-40 billion from the diaspora. Here is how the scheme works and what to watch out for.
body:
On Friday, the Reserve Bank of India did something it has not done since the rupee crisis of 2013. It told banks it would bear the full hedging cost on three-year to five-year foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians. By Monday, banks were already racing to turn that guarantee into the most aggressive dollar deposit pitch the diaspora has seen in over a decade.

Punjab National Bank's CEO Ashok Chandra told Reuters that the banking sector could raise $35 billion to $40 billion through the scheme. PNB alone is targeting $2.5 to $3 billion and plans to market the deposits "aggressively" across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the Middle East. Other lenders are not far behind: Indian Bank, Canara Bank, and Central Bank of India estimate total inflows between $20 billion and $25 billion, while Federal Bank projects up to $30 billion.

The numbers are large because the economics are unusually favourable — for both sides.

## How the Scheme Works

FCNR(B) deposits — Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Banks) deposits — let NRIs park US dollars, British pounds, euros, or other major currencies in Indian banks without converting to rupees. The deposits earn interest in the same foreign currency, and the principal is returned in that currency at maturity. There is no exchange-rate risk for the depositor.

The catch, historically, has been the rate. Until now, FCNR deposits typically offered around 3.5 per cent — well below what a US high-yield savings account or Treasury bill would pay. The economics did not work.

What changed is the RBI's decision to absorb the hedging cost. When a bank takes in a dollar deposit, it needs to hedge against rupee-dollar fluctuations. That hedging premium — currently steep because of rupee volatility — eats into the rate the bank can offer. By absorbing that cost, the RBI effectively lets banks offer rates above US Treasury yields, which currently sit at 4.2 per cent for three-year notes and 4.27 per cent for five-year notes.

Chandra confirmed that PNB's rate "will be higher than the US Treasury rate." He declined to specify the exact number, but market analysts expect rates in the 4.5 to 5.5 per cent range — competitive with the best US fixed-income options and significantly better than what NRIs have been offered in years.

## Why the RBI Is Doing This

The rupee fell to 95.71 against the dollar on Monday, reversing nearly all of Friday's rally. It has breached 96 in intraday trading this month — a record low. The currency has lost over 5 per cent this year, making it Asia's worst performer.

The pressure is coming from everywhere. Brent crude jumped above $96 after Israel launched fresh strikes on Lebanon, India's current account deficit is widening, foreign portfolio investors have pulled ₹2.67 lakh crore from Indian equities in 2026 — more than all of last year — and the prospect of a US Federal Reserve rate hike is pulling capital toward dollar assets.

The FCNR window is the RBI's attempt to fight these outflows by tapping the one reliable source of dollar inflows India has: its diaspora. The 2013 scheme, launched under similar circumstances, brought in over $34 billion in months and helped stabilise the rupee. The central bank is betting that history will repeat.

## What NRIs Should Consider

The window closes on September 30, 2026. Here is what matters.

**The rates are real.** Unlike NRE or NRO deposits, FCNR deposits pay in foreign currency. There is no rupee conversion risk. If an NRI deposits $100,000 at 5 per cent for three years, they will receive approximately $115,000 at maturity — in dollars.

**The lock-in is rigid.** FCNR deposits require a minimum three-year term under this scheme. Premature withdrawal is possible but may involve penalties and loss of the subsidised rate. This is not money you should need before 2029.

**The tax treatment matters.** Interest on FCNR deposits is tax-free in India for NRIs. However, US-resident NRIs must report the interest as income on their US tax returns. The effective after-tax return depends on your marginal tax bracket.

**Bank choice matters.** Larger banks — SBI, PNB, Bank of Baroda — tend to have established NRI desk infrastructure in major diaspora markets. Private banks like Federal Bank and HDFC may offer more competitive rates but could have different terms. Compare across at least three banks before committing.

**The rupee direction matters for repatriation.** If you eventually plan to convert the maturity proceeds to rupees — for a property purchase, for example — the rate at which the rupee trades in 2029 will determine your effective return. If the rupee weakens further, your dollars buy more. If it recovers, the pure dollar return is still competitive.

## The Bigger Picture

The RBI's FCNR window is not just a deposit product. It is a signal. The central bank is telling markets that it considers the current rupee weakness serious enough to deploy crisis-era tools. For NRIs, it also represents a rare moment when the economic interests of the depositor and the central bank are perfectly aligned.

The window is open. The rates have not been this good since 2013. Whether that is enough to pull $35 billion from diaspora bank accounts in the next four months will depend on how aggressively banks market the scheme — and how much NRIs trust that the money will be there in three years.

Given the RBI's track record on the 2013 scheme, where every depositor was made whole, the answer to that question is likely yes.
